claims.text: GPT-4o generated fabricated citations at an overall rate of 19.9% across six mental health literature reviews.
Among non-fabricated citations generated by GPT-4o, 45.4% contained at least one bibliographic error.
Digital object identifiers (DOIs) were the most common bibliographic error type among real journal citations generated by GPT-4o.
Citation fabrication rates in GPT-4o outputs differed significantly across mental disorders based on research maturity and public visibility.
Specialized prompt reviews produced a significantly higher citation fabrication rate than general overview reviews for binge eating disorder.

evidence.description: Across the 6 reviews, GPT-4o generated 176 citations, of which 35 (19.9%) were fabricated.
Among the 141 real citations generated by GPT-4o, 64 (45.4%) contained errors.
The highest error rate among nonfabricated journal citations was observed for DOIs (51/135, 37.8%).

Fabrication rates differed significantly by disorder (χ2 = 13.7; P = .001), with major depressive disorder at 6% (4/68), binge eating disorder at 28% (17/60), and body dysmorphic disorder at 29% (14/48).
Stratified analyses showed higher fabrication for specialized versus general reviews of binge eating disorder (11/24, 46% vs 6/36, 17%; P = .01).

methodologies.name: Factorial Prompting and Citation Verification Framework
methodologies.description: GPT-4o was prompted to generate six literature reviews across three mental disorders varying in public visibility and two review specificity levels, followed by manual citation verification across multiple scholarly databases.

limitations.text: The findings are based on three selected psychiatric conditions and may not generalize to other psychiatric disorders or specialized subfields.
Findings are specific to GPT-4o and may not generalize to outputs generated by other large language models.
The study evaluated standardized, straightforward prompts without implementing prompt engineering strategies such as retrieval-augmented or chain-of-thought prompting.
The evaluation analyzed a single generated output per prompt and did not assess intraprompt stochastic variability across multiple runs.

future_work.text: Assess whether similar patterns of citation fabrication and bibliographic errors occur across a broader range of mental health topics and other academic disciplines.
Investigate whether different large language models exhibit comparable citation fabrication patterns or model-specific reliability differences.
Test whether prompt engineering techniques like citation verification prompts reduce hallucination and citation error rates.
Examine multiple generations per prompt to evaluate the consistency and reproducibility of LLM-generated citations.
